title: Justice, excellence, giving to kin
hook: Allah commands justice, excellence and giving to kin (16:90), recited in many Friday sermons

segments.voice: Yesterday, the bee, guided to build and eat and make a drink of many colors. Your line was healing in it. What did you notice that did you good? Day four hundred fifty-four.

If you've ever sat through a Friday prayer in a mosque, you may have heard this verse without knowing its number. In mosques from Cairo to Chicago, imams often close the second half of the sermon with it, just before the call to stand for prayer. Week after week, the same few lines. A tradition says this custom goes back to the Umayyad ruler Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. Whatever the sermon was about, the week ends on these words. Today: the verse the sermon comes home to.

Pickthall translates it: "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness, and giving to kinsfolk, and forbiddeth lewdness and abomination and wickedness. He exhorteth you in order that ye may take heed." Three things commanded, three forbidden. Look at the three commanded. First, 'adl: justice. The root carries the sense of balance, of making two sides level, the way a scale settles. Justice is giving each person what is due to them, no more and no less, including the people you don't like. Second, ihsan. Pickthall says kindness; others say excellence, or doing what is beautiful. In a famous hadith, the angel Jibril asks the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ what ihsan is, and he answers: to worship God as though you see Him, and if you don't see Him, He sees you. So ihsan is justice with something added: doing more than what's owed, and doing it well, as if someone were watching who matters. Third, giving to kin. Not giving in general, though the Qur'an asks for that too. Giving to the near ones, the relatives. Notice the order: the scale, then the extra, then the people closest to you, who are often the hardest to be fair to. A saying attributed to the companion Ibn Mas'ud calls this the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for good and for evil. And a hadith in Tirmidhi says charity to a relative counts twice: once as charity, once as keeping the family tie. Then the three forbidden: shameful acts, munkar, what is known to be wrong, and baghy, overstepping against others. The verse closes not with a threat but with a reason: He counsels you, so that you might remember.
screen: `THREE COMMANDED, THREE FORBIDDEN.` · `'ADL: THE LEVEL SCALE.` · `IHSAN: AS IF YOU SEE HIM.` · `GIVING TO THE NEAR ONES.` · then, large: `JUSTICE, EXCELLENCE, KIN.`

segments.voice: The practice is to give something to a relative. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Picture your family, the whole loose circle of it: parents, siblings, cousins, an aunt you haven't called in a year. Let one face come forward. What could you give them this week? It could be money if they need it, but it could also be time, a meal, a message, a fair hearing in an old argument. Choose one. If you pray, you can ask for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Justice. 'Adl, the level scale, first of three things the verse commands, followed by excellence and giving to kin. Today's word.
Your line: justice, excellence, kin. Today, give the one thing you chose to that relative, or set a time to do it, and do it a little better than you'd have to. Day four hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: In many mosques the imam recites 16:90 at the end of the Friday sermon before the prayer begins; Muslims cite it as a summary of social ethics and give charity to relatives as both charity and keeping family ties.
